children: OTTAWA--The chief executive of one of Canada's biggest pension funds with experience in transport logistics abroad said she is interested in striking a deal with Ottawa to invest in the country's biggest airports.

"We're well suited for the opportunity," Deborah Orida, president and CEO of the Public Service Pension Investment Board, said in an interview Tuesday on the sidelines at an investment summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Earlier in the day, Carney said Canada is ready to open the doors for private-sector investment in the country's four biggest airports, with cash raised to be deployed in crucial infrastructure that Canada needs.

The pension fund, also known as PSP Investments, owns seven airports, mostly in Europe, through its AviAlliance subsidiary. "We are not only an airport investor but also an airport operator," Orida said. "That makes us, I think, well positioned to participate."

PSP Investments has 320 billion Canadian dollars (US$230.2 billion) under management, and in 2025 delivered a one-year net return of 6.5% and a 10-year net annualized return of 8.8%. It is tasked with delivering returns for federal-government employees, members of the Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

As envisaged by Carney, the airport deals would be set up as long-term concessions, which are agreements under which the private-sector investor handles the operation and maintenance of the airport for a set period. Current Canadian laws dissuade private-sector investments in airports, which are run by not-for-profit, non-share capital authorities that fund operations through fees charged to passengers and airlines.

Orida said PSP's AviAlliance has a track record that shows it can modernize airport terminals and expand route networks through its contact with airlines. The airports in the PSP portfolio include those in Athens, Glasgow and San Juan, Puerto Rico.

"We have the opportunity with our operating expertise to generate value that is not coming at the expense of the customers," Orida said. She added that the airports are a key holding in their infrastructure class, which over a five-year period has recorded average annual returns of about 15%.

According to Statistics Canada, the country's airports served 158.9 million passengers last year, with Toronto's Pearson International by far the largest, accounting for nearly 30% of passenger traffic.

The prior Liberal government administration, under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, had an interest in encouraging more domestic investment by pension funds--drawing criticism from some pension-fund executives about any formal effort to compel asset managers to reallocate money from higher-returning opportunities.

Orida said Carney's airport announcement signals the government is looking to make good-investment opportunities more readily available for large investors like PSP. Prior to the summit, PSP unveiled plans to increase its domestic holdings by up to 40%, and cross the C$100 billion threshold in the next few years.
That pledge was driven by private-investing opportunities, "and the attractiveness of the Canadian public equities for our portfolio, rather than a government edict," she said.

Canada's largest pension fund, the CPP Investment Board, said Tuesday it would join forces with Brookfield Asset Management on a C$50 billion fund seeking opportunities in infrastructure. Prior to the summit, the five biggest Canadian banks pledged a collective C$320 billion in capital for the domestic economy.
